slides.title: The intelligence *ladder*
slides.text: When an AI system is not good enough, what do you change first?

narration: When an AI system is not good enough, there are eight things you can change.
They are not equally sensible to try.
This video shows the order worth trying them in.

slides.caption: When an AI system is not good enough, there are eight things you can change. They are not equally sensible to try.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: Changing the system around the AI

narration: Here is what this video covers.
We start with two simple words you will need.
Then we look at why the order of changes matters.
Next, three changes to the system around the AI.
Then five changes to the AI itself.
Last, how to measure every change.
That is how you know what worked.

slides.caption: This video covers why the order matters. Then three changes around the AI, five changes to the AI itself, and how to measure.

slides.title: What a *model* is
slides.text: It reads the words you give it and writes words back.
slides.picture: A small rounded device with a plain sheet going in on one side and a written sheet coming out the other.

narration: At the heart of any AI system is a program that reads text and writes text back.
You give it words, and it answers with words.
This program is called the model.

slides.caption: At the heart of any AI system is a program that reads text and writes text back. It is called the model.

slides.title: An *agent* gets a task done
slides.text: A system around the model that lets it take actions.
slides.picture: The small device inside a simple frame, moving along stepping stones towards a folder.

narration: A model on its own only writes answers.
Often we want more. We want it to finish a whole task.
So we build a system around the model.
It lets the model take actions, one step after another.
This is called an agent.

slides.caption: A model on its own only writes answers. An agent is a system built around the model. It lets the model take actions to finish a task.

slides.title: "The model is not *good enough*"
slides.text: This is usually said before anyone has measured what is failing.
slides.picture: A hand pointing at the device while a magnifying glass lies unused beside it.

narration: Now you know what a model and an agent are.
So why does the order of changes matter?
When an agent fails, a common first reaction is to blame the model.
People say the model is not good enough.
But that does not say what is actually wrong.
It is usually said before anyone has measured what is failing.

slides.caption: Saying the model is not good enough does not say what is wrong. It is usually said before anyone has measured what is failing.

slides.title: Training too early *costs more* than money
items: The real fault is still there

narration: The usual answer is to change the model itself.
You feed it new examples, and it learns from them.
This is called training.
Training too early costs a lot of money.
It also makes the system heavier.
And it can tie you to one model.
You now have a trained model to look after.
And the real fault is still sitting there underneath.

slides.caption: Changing the model with new examples is called training. Too early, it wastes money, makes the system heavier and ties you to one model. The real fault stays.

slides.title: The cheap changes *keep paying off*
slides.text: Better wording and better information keep finding gains.
slides.picture: A pencil on a sheet of paper beside a row of small blocks that keep getting taller.

narration: Published work points the other way.
Better wording and better information for the model are cheap to try.
They keep finding gains that teams thought were used up.
The expensive changes often fix something that was never the problem.

slides.caption: Published work shows better wording and better information keep finding gains. Expensive changes often fix something that was never the problem.

slides.title: There are *eight* things you can change

narration: We saw why jumping to training too early is costly.
Now, here are all eight things you can change.
The first three change the system around the model.
The model itself stays exactly the same.
The last five change the model itself.
These are the expensive ones.

slides.caption: There are eight things you can change. The first three change the system around the model. The last five change the model itself.

slides.title: Deck A is a *ladder*
slides.text: Finish each step before the next one is worth trying.

narration: The first three work like a ladder.
You climb them in order.
Finish each step before the next one is worth trying.
We call this group Deck A.

slides.caption: The first three changes run in order, like a ladder. Finish each step before the next one is worth trying. This group is Deck A.

slides.title: Step 1: *Instructions*
slides.text: The wording of the task.
slides.gate: Accuracy climbs for a week of prompt work, then goes flat

narration: Step one is the instructions.
You write words that tell the model what the task is.
Those words are called the prompt.
Keep improving the prompt.
Measure how often the answers are right.
Move on when that climbs for a week of work, then goes flat.

slides.caption: Step 1 is the wording that tells the model the task, called the prompt. Move on when accuracy climbs for a week, then goes flat.

slides.title: Step 2: *Context*
slides.text: What reaches the model, including what it remembers.
slides.gate: Beats a plain version, and failures are about acting

narration: Step two is context.
Everything that reaches the model along with the task is called context.
It includes your documents, and what the agent remembers from before.
First, your way of preparing documents must beat a plain, simple version.
Test both on the same cases. That keeps it fair.
Then move on when the failures left are about taking action, not missing knowledge.

slides.caption: Step 2 changes what reaches the model, including memory. Move on when it beats a plain version and the failures left are about acting.

slides.title: An agent works in a *loop*

narration: Before step three, one more idea.
An agent works in rounds. First, it picks an action.
Then it looks at the result.
Then it decides what to do next, and goes round again.
This repeating cycle is called the loop.

slides.caption: An agent works in rounds. It picks an action, looks at the result and decides what to do next. This cycle is called the loop.

slides.title: Step 3: *Tools and the loop*
slides.text: The system that runs the model and lets it act.
slides.gate: Each round is recorded, and what fails is knowing your field

narration: Step three is the tools and the loop.
The agent can do things, like search a file or save a note.
Each of these abilities is called a tool.
Record every round of the loop.
Then you can trace what happened.
Move on when what still fails is the model not knowing your field.

slides.caption: Step 3 changes the tools and the loop that let the model act. Move on when every round is recorded and what fails is knowing your field.

slides.title: Step 3 is the one *most often skipped*
slides.text: Teams go from good context straight to training.
slides.picture: A short three-rung ladder with its top rung untouched, and the device leaping from the middle rung to a heavy crate.

narration: Of the three steps, step three is the one most often skipped.
Teams see that the context is good, but the agent still fails.
So they jump straight to training.

slides.caption: Step 3 is the most skipped step. Teams with good context that still fails often jump straight to training.

slides.title: The loop *changes the decisions*
slides.text: Keep the task and model fixed. A different loop still changes decisions.
slides.picture: Two identical devices with the same sheet, each on a different looping path that ends at a different door.

narration: Published work kept the task and the model fixed, and changed only the loop.
The agent made different decisions.
That happened even when the success rate looked the same.
For tasks that are mostly about finding information, the loop can matter more than how the search is built.
Most teams who think they need a trained model need better tools and a better loop.

slides.caption: Changing only the loop changes what an agent decides. Most teams who think they need a trained model need better tools and a better loop.

slides.title: Teach *behaviour* with examples
slides.text: Show the model many tasks paired with good answers.
slides.picture: Pairs of cards flowing in a line into the small device.

narration: That was Deck A.
Now we turn to changing the model itself.
One way is to show the model thousands of examples.
Each example is a task paired with a good answer.
The model learns to behave like the examples.
This is called fine-tuning.

slides.caption: Showing the model thousands of tasks paired with good answers teaches it how to behave. This is called fine-tuning.

slides.title: Teach *knowledge* with raw text
slides.text: Let the model keep reading your own documents.
slides.picture: A tall stack of plain documents with pages drifting into the small device.

narration: There is a second way to teach a model.
A model first learns by reading a huge amount of text.
You can let it keep reading, using your own documents.
It learns the words and ideas of your field.
This is called continued pretraining.

slides.caption: A model first learns by reading huge amounts of text. Letting it keep reading your own documents is called continued pretraining.

slides.title: Behaviour and knowledge are *different jobs*

right.head: Continued pretraining
rows: Wrong tool for format or tone

narration: Now put the two side by side.
Teaching a model how to behave and teaching it about your field are different jobs.
Fine-tuning learns from thousands of examples.
Continued pretraining learns from raw text. That just means plain documents.
It needs billions of small pieces of words.
Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves.
Continued pretraining changes what it knows, and how it reads your language.
So fine-tuning is the wrong tool for adding knowledge.
And continued pretraining is the wrong tool for fixing format or tone.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning learns behaviour from example pairs. Continued pretraining learns your field from raw text. Each is the wrong tool for the other job.

slides.title: Most companies have lots of *raw text*
slides.text: They often have very few examples with good answers.
slides.picture: A very tall stack of documents next to one tiny pair of cards.

narration: This matters for most companies.
A company with lots of its own documents has plenty of raw text.
But it often has very few example pairs.
That makes continued pretraining the natural option for it.
It also explains why so many fine-tuning projects disappoint.
The wrong tool was picked for the problem.

slides.caption: A company with lots of its own documents has raw text but few example pairs. That is why many fine-tuning projects disappoint.

slides.title: Specific facts stay *out of the model*
slides.text: They live in documents the agent looks up, and in memory.
slides.picture: The device on one side and a separate open file box, with one card lifted out.

narration: One more point about both methods.
Some facts are about one customer, one case or one policy.
Those facts belong in neither method.
They stay in documents the agent looks up, and in the agent's governed memory.
There, each fact can be shown with its source, updated or deleted.
A trained model cannot do any of those things.

slides.caption: Facts about one customer, case or policy stay in documents and the agent's memory. There they can be shown, updated and deleted. A trained model cannot.

slides.title: Deck B is *not* a ladder
slides.text: Read what is failing, then pick the change that fits.
slides.picture: The device with five short paths fanning out from it, one path highlighted.

narration: We saw two different ways to teach a model.
Now, how to choose among the five changes to the model.
These five do not run in order.
You look at what is failing, and pick the change that fits.
You may need more than one.
We call this group Deck B.

slides.caption: The five model changes do not run in order. Read what is failing, pick the change that fits, and expect to combine them. This group is Deck B.

slides.title: Wrong behaviour? *Adapters and fine-tuning*
slides.text: Train a small add-on that sits on top of the model.
slides.picture: A large locked block with a thin strip plugging into its top.

narration: The first symptom is wrong format, tone or task behaviour.
The fix is to teach new behaviour with fine-tuning.
You do not have to change the whole model.
You can train a small add-on that sits on top of it.
This add-on is called an adapter.

slides.caption: Wrong format, tone or behaviour points to fine-tuning. A small add-on trained on top of the model is called an adapter.

slides.title: Too slow or costly? *Distillation*
slides.text: A large model teaches a smaller, cheaper one.
slides.picture: A large device passing a card to a much smaller device.

narration: The second symptom is different.
The answers are good, but the model is too slow or too expensive.
Then a large model can teach a smaller, cheaper model to give the same answers.
This is called distillation.

slides.caption: When answers are good but too slow or costly, a large model can teach a smaller, cheaper one. This is called distillation.

slides.title: Wrong judgement? *Reinforcement fine-tuning*
slides.text: The model learns from scores on results that can be checked.
slides.picture: The device beside three attempts on paper, one of them marked with a star.

narration: The third symptom is right format, but wrong judgement.
The answer looks right, but the decision in it is wrong.
This fix needs results that can be checked and scored.
The model tries, gets a score, and does more of what scored well.
This is called reinforcement fine-tuning.

slides.caption: Right format but wrong judgement points to reinforcement fine-tuning. The model learns from scores. So the results must be checkable.

slides.title: Misreads your field? *Continued pretraining*
slides.text: Let the model keep reading your own documents.

narration: The fourth symptom is about understanding.
The model does not understand the words, documents or symbols of your field.
We met this fix earlier.
Let the model keep reading your own text with continued pretraining.

slides.caption: When the model misreads the words, documents or symbols of your field, look at continued pretraining. It lets the model keep reading your text.

slides.title: Data is not text? *Custom architecture*
slides.text: A model built specially for that kind of data.
slides.picture: A web of connected dots and a wavy signal line beside a specially shaped device.

narration: The last symptom is about the data itself.
Sometimes your data is not text at all.
It might be a web of connections, long sequences, or signals, in huge amounts.
Then look at a model built specially for that kind of data.
This is called a custom architecture.

slides.caption: When your data is webs of connections, sequences or signals, look at a model built for that data. This is called a custom architecture.

slides.title: Pick by *symptom*
pairs: Right quality, too slow or costly

narration: Here is the whole map in one place.
Wrong format, tone or behaviour points to adapters and fine-tuning.
Too slow or too costly points to distillation.
Wrong judgement points to reinforcement fine-tuning.
Misreading your field points to continued pretraining.
Data that is not text points to custom architecture.

slides.caption: Read the symptom and go to the matching change: adapters, distillation, reinforcement, continued pretraining or a custom architecture.

slides.title: The options *combine*

narration: These options often combine.
A standard pairing is continued pretraining, then fine-tuning.
The first teaches the field. The second teaches the task.
Distillation can come after any of the others.
It makes the final model smaller and cheaper to run.

slides.caption: Options combine. Continued pretraining teaches the field, then fine-tuning teaches the task. Distillation can follow any of them.

slides.title: Every step is a *measurement*
slides.text: You need an evaluation suite that you own.
slides.picture: A closed, locked box of index cards with a plain ruler in front and the device beside it.

narration: That covers all eight changes.
Now, the one thing every change depends on.
Every decision to move on is based on a measurement.
So you need a fixed set of real cases with known correct answers.
You own it, and you test every change against it.
This is called an evaluation suite.
Without one, teams pick changes based on stories.
And stories favour whatever is most fashionable.

slides.caption: Every decision on the ladder needs a measurement. A fixed set of real cases with known answers is called an evaluation suite.

slides.title: How to build the *suite*
items: Owned by experts in your field

narration: Here is how to build that suite.
Build it from real failures, not imagined ones.
Build it before the agent, not after.
Have experts in your field own it.
They know what a correct answer looks like.

slides.caption: Build the suite from real failures, before the agent is built. Experts in your field should own it. They know what a correct answer looks like.

slides.title: If the agent *remembers*, test memory
items: A fact that changed over time
A question the record cannot answer
Someone not allowed to see it

narration: Some agents keep a memory from one task to the next.
If yours does, the suite also tests what memory can break.
Test a fact that changed over time.
Test a question the record cannot answer.
Test a record that was deleted.
And test a person who is not allowed to see it.

slides.caption: If the agent keeps memory, test what memory breaks. Try a changed fact, an unanswerable question, a deleted record and someone not allowed to see it.

slides.title: Beats careful people? *Treat it as an alarm*
slides.text: The system learned to score well without doing the job.
slides.picture: The device wearing a big ribbon medal, with untouched task papers behind it and a small warning light.

narration: One warning belongs here.
Sometimes a score comes out higher than a careful person gets on the same task.
That means the system learned to score well without doing the job.
This is called reward hacking.
Treat it as an alarm.
Check how the score is given before you trust it.

slides.caption: A score above careful human performance is an alarm. The system learned to score well without doing the job. Check the scoring first.

slides.title: What this *rests on*
items: Deck A: partly our own measurements
Deck B: published work, vendor documents
Two decks: the author's own view

narration: Before we finish, a note on the evidence.
Deck A rests partly on our own measurements.
Deck B comes from published work, and from the companies that make the models.
Splitting the eight changes into two decks is my own view.

slides.caption: Deck A rests partly on our own measurements. Deck B comes from published work and vendor documents. The two-deck split is the author's own view.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: Change the system before the model
Behaviour and knowledge need different data
Measure every change on real cases

narration: Here is what to remember.
First, change the system before you change the model.
Deck A runs in order and costs little.
The evidence says most of the gain is still there.
Deck B is picked by what is failing.
It costs more, and it adds a model you must look after.
Teaching behaviour and teaching knowledge are different jobs.
They need different kinds of data.
Measure every change against real cases with known answers.
The next video is Step 1, Instructions.

slides.caption: Change the system before the model. Climb Deck A in order and pick Deck B by symptom. Behaviour and knowledge need different data. Measure every change.

sections.heading: Behaviour and knowledge are different jobs
